parts.note: PR is the standard abbreviation for Puerto Rico
to expel someone is to oust them

explanation.surface: An island territory throws out an unwelcome author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' looks like part of a sentence about Puerto Rico acting, but it only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcel Proust was the French novelist who wrote In Search of Lost Time, so he is an example of a writer.

indicators.note: poor suggests something in bad shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sorry father has been dosed with some chemical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the' reads as introducing the definition but its letters are needed in the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A phosphate is a chemical compound, a salt of phosphoric acid, used in fertilisers and detergents.

parts.note: surface: matches that the media do not report or broadcast; setter's reading: no roof overhead, so played in the open air

explanation.walkthrough: 'coverage' means media reporting on the surface but a literal roof in the cryptic reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Games played in the open air rather than in a hall or under a roof are described as being played outside.

clue.text: Examination by riddle would-be film star must undergo

parts.note: a riddle is a coarse sieve, and to screen is to sieve
an examination is a test

explanation.surface: An aspiring actor must sit an exam set as a puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'riddle' looks like a puzzle; it is a coarse sieve for gravel or soil. 'by' means placed beside.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspiring film actors are filmed in a trial performance to judge their suitability before casting.

clue.text: Brisk single — looked sharp about it too

parts.note: surface padding: a run in cricket, contributing no letters

indicators.note: about means going around, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: to spire is to rise to a sharp point, as a church steeple does
taken as written
surface padding, contributing no letters

explanation.surface: A quick run in cricket, with someone glancing alertly around as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'looked sharp' suggests being alert, but it means pointed upwards like a steeple. The words 'single' and 'too' add nothing to the wordplay and seem to be padding, or a slip in the printed clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirited and brisk both describe something lively, energetic and full of vigour, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Nightingale, when preceding a princess of Athens

parts.note: Philomel is a poetic name for the nightingale
taken as written

explanation.surface: A songbird placed before royalty from ancient Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth this princess was turned into a nightingale, which is why poets call the bird Philomel.
explanation.definitionFit: Philomela was a daughter of King Pandion of Athens in Greek myth, so she was an Athenian princess.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a loud style of popular music

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a listener's verdict that some music is difficult; 'hard' is a separate meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a genre of popular music and also, in rock-hard or rock solid, describes firmness.

parts.note: ta is British informal for thanks
a sting is a sharp pain

explanation.surface: Learning from experience, all because of suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thanks to' reads as one phrase meaning because of; 'to' is only the link.
explanation.definitionFit: To taste something is to experience it, as in tasting success, so tasting is having experience of it.

clue.text: Father may become divine in time

indicators.note: in places one word inside another

parts.note: a day is a period of time
DD is Doctor of Divinity, and a divine is a clergyman

explanation.surface: A priest may in time rise to holiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Father' looks like a priest and 'divine' like holy; a divine is a theologian, abbreviated DD.
explanation.definitionFit: Daddy is the familiar, childish word for one's father, an informal synonym.

clue.text: Kashmir, where an ice-floe starts the picture river

indicators.note: starts points to the beginnings of words, their opening letters

parts.note: opening letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A floe of ice heralds a film set by a river in Kashmir.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is the film The Bridge on the River Kwai.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1957 film The Bridge on the River Kwai is named after the river in Thailand where it is set.

clue.text: On strike to get increase, become too big for one's boots, perhaps

definitions.text: become too big for one's boots, perhaps

parts.note: workers on strike are out
to increase is to grow

explanation.surface: Workers walk out for a pay rise and get above themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'increase' reads as a pay increase, the usual aim of a strike, but here it is a verb. The 'perhaps' marks the definition as one example: you outgrow boots literally, as a child does.
explanation.definitionFit: A child who outgrows shoes has literally become too big for them, the literal version of the idiom about conceit.

clue.text: Cut in, so returned to Edward

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read from right to left

parts.note: sic is Latin for so or thus, used to mark a quotation as printed
Ed is the short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: Someone was allowed into a deal, and the share went back to Edward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut in' looks like one phrase meaning to interrupt; in fact 'Cut' alone is the definition and 'in' is the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Incised means carved or engraved with a sharp edge, so it is a past-tense synonym of cut.

clue.text: Ancestor gives pointer to go right maybe

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters are only one possible arrangement, so they may be shuffled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: An old forebear offers a tip on which way to turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pointer to go right' reads as a direction sign; every letter of it is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A progenitor is a direct ancestor from whom a family line descends, so the words are synonyms.

indicators.note: sounds tells us to go by how a word is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: limey is American and Australian slang for an English person

explanation.surface: A British accent compared with chalky tap water.
explanation.walkthrough: Limey, from the lime juice once given to British sailors, is slang for a Briton.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard water carries dissolved calcium from limestone, so it is limy, full of lime.

clue.text: Can be gripping, hanging around the lady's back

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one word goes outside the other

parts.note: pensile means hanging down

indicators.note: back means going backwards, so the word is read right to left

parts.note: her is the possessive for a lady

explanation.surface: A tense drama with a woman's back shown hanging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gripping' sounds like thrilling, but it means able to grasp, the way a monkey's tail can.
explanation.definitionFit: A prehensile tail or limb can grasp and hold things, as a monkey's tail can.

parts.note: A and E are two of the musical notes A to G
to assess something is to rate it

explanation.surface: Musical notes are graded, compared with geological specimens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minerals' suggests rocks, but here it means mineral waters, the bottled drinks that are often fizzy.
explanation.definitionFit: Some mineral waters are sparkling, charged with gas bubbles, which is what aerated means.

clue.text: Finds entertainment with some poetry? Not quite

indicators.note: not quite means falling just short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a disco is a dance, a form of entertainment
verse is poetry

explanation.surface: Someone finds amusement in reading poems, or nearly.
explanation.walkthrough: VERSE loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To discover something is to find it for the first time, so discovers is a verb synonym of finds.

indicators.note: something exploded is blown apart, so the letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone lost their temper and blew up.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition while the word angered, blown apart, supplies the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To be enraged is to be made furious, so a person getting angered until they explode has become enraged.

indicators.note: spilt suggests contents spread out in disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Fuel has leaked, so the vehicle must sit unused.
explanation.definitionFit: Diesel oil is the heavy petroleum fuel burnt in diesel engines in lorries, buses and ships.

parts.note: ex means former or old
an attitude is a posture, a pose

explanation.surface: People reveal their outdated opinions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They show up' looks like a verb phrase about people arriving; it is a noun definition for exposés, the pieces of journalism that show people up.
explanation.definitionFit: Exposés are reports revealing scandal or wrongdoing, so they are things that show up their subjects.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: indicated direction with a finger
second meaning: a remark made sharply and deliberately

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one guide leading emphatically; the clue splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the past tense of point, to indicate a direction, and an adjective for sharply emphatic remarks.

clue.text: Successfully conclude account with serpent's original greeting

parts.note: AC is the abbreviation for account
what the serpent in Eden might have said to the first woman: hi plus her name

explanation.surface: Finishing a bank account with a snake's old hello.
explanation.walkthrough: 'original' points to Eve as the first woman, whom the serpent addressed in Eden.
explanation.definitionFit: To achieve is to accomplish or bring something to a successful end, a verb synonym of successfully conclude.

clue.text: Send out Oriental servant, having dined

parts.note: E for East, the Orient
a manservant is a man
to dine is to eat

explanation.surface: Dismissing an Eastern servant after the meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send out' sounds like dismissing the servant; it means to give off, as light or a smell does.
explanation.definitionFit: To emanate is to issue or give off, as a smell or light emanates from a source.

definitions.meaning: salve is the Latin, so classical, word of greeting
frozen pellets of rain falling from the sky

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned ointment as a remedy against the elements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'salve' reads as an ointment; it is the Latin greeting, so 'Classic' means classical.
explanation.definitionFit: Salve in Latin is a greeting like hail, and hail is also icy precipitation, a kind of bad weather.

clue.text: Cruel Shah, right to be ruined

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A tyrannical Persian ruler deserves his downfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Harsh and cruel both describe treatment that is severe and unkind, so the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Maybe whisky measures swallowed in study time

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart

indicators.note: something swallowed goes inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a date is a point in time
ens are printers' measures of width

explanation.surface: Tots of whisky downed during a study period.
explanation.walkthrough: 'measures' suggests shots of whisky, but these are the printer's en measures, units of type width.
explanation.definitionFit: Whisky is distilled, the vapour cooled back into liquid, so the spirit is an example of a condensate.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: made of ..., pine or fir boards
second meaning: ..., a seaside town in Kent, England

explanation.walkthrough: As an adjective, a deal table is made of softwood planks. Deal is also a coastal town in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: Deal is fir or pine timber, and deal furniture is made of it; Deal is also an English coastal place.

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
on means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A piece of writing about mysteries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the unknown' sounds like mystery; it is the anonymous author credited on a poem or quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon, short for anonymous, is the credit given to an author whose name is not known.

indicators.note: perhaps signals the word is one possibility, so its letters can be arranged differently

parts.note: re means about or concerning
the word unite with its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A call to come together, trailing into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' looks like an ellipsis lead-in to the next clue; it is a noun meaning a body of followers.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is a group of attendants accompanying an important person, which is a following in the noun sense.

parts.note: surface: an inspiring instruction to an orchestra; setter's reading: stirred up, excited, describing how the music should be played

explanation.walkthrough: Continuing from the previous clue, 'stirring' sounds like rousing; in fact it describes a restless, agitated manner of playing.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitato is the Italian tempo marking telling performers to play in an agitated, restless and excited way.

clue.text: Fellow caught in hold-up is a pleasure-seeker

indicators.note: caught in means trapped inside, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: a heist is a robbery, a hold-up
a don is a university fellow

explanation.surface: A man trapped in a robbery turns out to love the high life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow' tempts you to use the usual HE, but here a Fellow of an Oxford or Cambridge college is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedonist lives for enjoyment and sensual gratification, so is a seeker of pleasure.

indicators.note: in places one word inside another

parts.note: authentic means real
VE Day, Victory in Europe, 8 May 1945, a fine day for Britain

explanation.surface: A quoted song title, from Madame Butterfly, staged as a genuine performance.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look like the aria from Puccini's opera; the fine day is the one celebrating victory in Europe in 1945.
explanation.definitionFit: To reveal something is to show it or make it visible, so the verb is a synonym.
